summary: The Internet Society's statement that the Internet is for everyone, but only if people make it so. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a short message saying that the Internet should belong to all people, and that we have to work to make that true.

subtitle: The Internet Society's call for universal, inclusive access to the global network.

tldr.problem: While the Internet is growing rapidly, it will only truly be available to everyone if we actively remove barriers to access and ensure fair policies.
tldr.mechanism: An ideological statement from Internet Society leadership calling for dedicated work on affordability, regulatory freedom, technological innovation, universal deployment, usability, legal harmonization, privacy protection, and responsible use.
tldr.outcome: The document serves as a rallying call for stakeholders to address the remaining gaps between the Internet's potential and its actual accessibility worldwide.

facts.label: World population with no phone access

today: RFC 3271 is an Informational document expressing the Internet Society's ideology from 2002. The call for universal access remains relevant: while global Internet penetration has increased dramatically since 2002, significant gaps in access persist, particularly in developing nations and among low-income populations.

sections.title: The Internet is for Everyone
sections.content:
Written in April 2002 by Vint Cerf, former chairman of the Internet Society, this document expresses the organization's core ideology: the Internet should serve all people worldwide.

At the time of writing, the Internet had been doubling in users annually since 1988, with over 150 million host computers and an estimated 513 million users. Projections suggested 1.5 billion Internet-enabled appliances would eventually connect, from pagers to personal digital assistants, alongside traditional computers. Despite this explosive growth, fewer than half of Earth's population had ever made a phone call, and most lacked Internet access.

The RFC frames the challenge plainly: the Internet has the potential to be the most powerful amplifier of human expression ever created, offering a global platform for voices that would otherwise be faint. However, this vision will only become reality if the Internet community consciously works to overcome the barriers of cost, regulation, complexity, and governance.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is growing super fast and reaching more people. But lots of people in the world still don't have it. The author says we need to work hard to make sure it's available and affordable for everyone.

sections.title: Key Barriers to Universal Access
sections.content:
The document identifies six critical barriers that prevent the Internet from truly being available to everyone.

Affordability: The Internet must become as affordable as other essential infrastructure. This requires not just relying on Moore's Law to reduce equipment costs, but also using regulatory policy to encourage competition.

Freedom from restriction: Governments must not restrict access to the network. The Internet requires unrestricted and unregulated operation, coupled with freedom of speech and freedom to receive information.

Technological capacity: The Internet must evolve to keep pace with explosive demand. Maintaining the Internet Architecture Board, the Internet Engineering Task Force and related standards bodies is essential to this ongoing development.

Universal deployment: The Internet must become accessible in every home, business, school, library, hospital and town worldwide, at any time and in every language.

Simplicity: Internet interfaces and tools must be simple enough for anyone to use, supported by education and training.

Responsible use: Users must employ the Internet with care and consideration for others' rights, while communities develop tools to prevent and address abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The author lists six big problems that keep people from using the Internet: it costs too much, governments block it, it's not fast enough, it's not everywhere, it's too hard to use, and people abuse it. Each one needs to be fixed.

sections.title: Specific Challenges
sections.content:
Beyond the six main barriers, the RFC addresses additional challenges that demand attention.

Legal harmonization: Incompatible laws across nations create obstacles to global electronic commerce, intellectual property protection, freedom of expression and economic development. A coordinated global legal framework that works across borders is necessary.

Cryptography and privacy: Users must be able to protect their privacy and transaction confidentiality. Cryptographic technology should be freely available, applicable and exportable to support this right. Authentication methods are equally vital to build trust in digital commerce.

Child protection: Parents and teachers need tools to create protected spaces online for young people, allowing adults to control what content children encounter. These protections must be voluntary and flexible rather than imposed uniformly.

Interplanetary expansion: The document optimistically notes that the Internet is expanding beyond Earth. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory was already developing the Interplanetary Internet, which by 2008 was expected to provide Earth-Mars communication as the foundation for an interplanetary network of networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Different countries have different laws that don't work well together. People need codes to keep their secrets safe online. Parents need ways to keep the Internet safe for kids. And the author thinks the Internet will even reach Mars one day.

sections.title: The Internet's Transformative Power
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes the Internet's unprecedented role in human communication and coordination. As a repository of human accomplishment, it is now the place where knowledge accumulates and is shared globally. Online databases and shared resources are accelerating the pace of scientific and technical progress.

The Internet also serves as a powerful tool for democratic participation. Proxy voting for stock shareholders was already common online, and the RFC suggests that similar innovations could extend Internet-enabled voting and political participation to broader populations.

The document celebrates the Internet as perhaps the most powerful amplifier of free speech ever invented. It enables multiple viewpoints and dialogue in ways that traditional, one-way mass media cannot achieve. This makes it essential to preserve the Internet's open, unrestricted character while also building systems to detect and punish abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is like the world's biggest library and town square combined. It helps scientists share discoveries, lets people vote online, and gives everyone a voice. That power is why we have to protect it and make it available to all.

sections.title: A Call to Commitment
sections.content:
The document concludes with a rallying cry for the Internet community to commit to universal access. The Internet Society launched a campaign with the slogan Internet is for everyone, but Cerf emphasizes that the slogan alone means nothing without sustained action.

Each barrier requires dedicated effort. Reducing costs requires both technological progress and regulatory reform. Preserving freedom requires vigilance against government overreach. Meeting demand requires investment in technical infrastructure and standards development. Achieving universal deployment requires infrastructure investment and localization into many languages.

Perhaps most importantly, the RFC reminds readers that technology alone cannot solve this challenge. The Internet will only be truly for everyone if humans commit to making it so through policy choices, business decisions, educational efforts and conscious responsibility in their use of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The author's main message is: we have to actually do the work. Just saying the Internet should be for everyone isn't enough. Every person, company and country needs to decide they will help make it happen.
